---
title: "A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction"
---

## How does an animal coordinate a response?

An animal detecting food, escaping a threat or reproducing must connect
information to action. Neural activity, endocrine signals and muscle do not
operate as isolated topics. They link sensory input and internal state to
effectors while using the transport and metabolic support developed in earlier
units. This unit builds those links from membrane properties to whole-organism
behaviour and reproductive regulation.

You should explain membrane potential and action potentials without confusing
voltage with ion concentration; trace a chemical synapse and a reflex pathway;
connect calcium, ATP and muscle force; distinguish hormone concentration from
target-cell response; and explain a reproductive feedback loop. Use the
[slides](lec.qmd), [exercises](exercise.qmd) and [quiz](quiz.qmd).

## Ion gradients create possibilities for electrical signals

A membrane potential is a voltage difference across a cell membrane. Ion
concentrations differ inside and outside cells, and membranes are selectively
permeable. The combined electrical and chemical tendencies determine each
ion's electrochemical driving force. Resting membranes are often more permeable
to some ions than others. ATP-dependent transport, including the sodium–potassium
pump in many animal cells, maintains gradients that leak pathways would
otherwise dissipate.

The inside of a resting neuron is commonly negative relative to the outside.
This does not mean that all intracellular material is negatively charged:
only a small charge separation near the membrane is needed for a voltage.
Opening a channel changes permeability; the direction of ion movement depends
on that ion's electrochemical gradient. A sodium channel is not itself an
ATP-driven sodium pump.

A small local electrical change may decay with distance. An **action potential**
is regenerated when voltage-dependent channels activate in adjacent membrane.
In a typical vertebrate axon, rapid sodium entry drives depolarisation and
subsequent channel changes, including potassium conductance, contribute to
repolarisation. Refractory properties limit immediate re-excitation and help
organise propagation. Exact waveforms and ion contributions differ among
cell types, so treat this as a representative mechanism, not a universal
recipe for every excitable cell. The supporting reading explains
[neuronal communication](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/35-2-how-neurons-communicate).

## A signal can be coded without becoming a larger spike

Once threshold is reached under comparable conditions, an individual action
potential is approximately stereotyped. Stronger stimulation can change firing
frequency, timing and the number of recruited neurons rather than making
each spike proportionately taller. A sensory neuron is also selective: receptor
properties and neural pathways determine what kind of change it can encode.
An electrical recording alone does not reveal the animal's conscious experience.

At a **chemical synapse**, arrival of an action potential can open presynaptic
calcium channels. Calcium entry promotes neurotransmitter release. Transmitter
acts on postsynaptic receptors, changing the receiving cell's activity. Effects
depend on receptor type and the target cell's conditions; the same transmitter
name is not a complete explanation of excitation or inhibition.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  S[Stimulus] --> R[Sensory receptor and afferent neuron]
  R --> I[Integration in neural circuit]
  I --> M[Motor neuron]
  M --> E[Muscle or other effector]
  E --> O[Response changes conditions]
```

This original reflex sketch shows a functional route rather than a detailed
anatomical circuit. A simple reflex can operate without waiting for conscious
decision, while information may also reach other brain regions. The existence
of a fast local pathway does not imply that the entire nervous system has
one linear input and one output. Integrating excitatory, inhibitory and
modulatory signals helps make context-dependent responses possible.

## Muscle converts chemical energy into force

Skeletal muscle contains fibres with organised contractile machinery. Within
sarcomeres, interactions between actin and myosin generate force through
cycles requiring ATP. Calcium exposes regulatory sites in the skeletal-muscle
thin filament by acting through troponin and tropomyosin. ATP binding permits
myosin to detach; ATP hydrolysis prepares subsequent interactions. Therefore
ATP is necessary for controlled cycling and relaxation as well as work.

At a vertebrate neuromuscular junction, motor-neuron signalling triggers a
muscle electrical response. That response reaches internal membrane systems
and promotes calcium release from intracellular stores. Calcium recovery helps
end activation. The sequence connects a neural signal to a mechanical effect:
it is more informative than saying “the nerve contracts the muscle”. OpenStax
provides a supporting account of
[muscle contraction](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/38-4-muscle-contraction-and-locomotion).

An **isometric** contraction develops force without an overall change in
muscle length. Mechanical work on a load requires displacement; for a constant
force aligned with movement, $W=Fd$. A muscle can consume ATP while holding
a load stationary even though the external mechanical work in that simple
calculation is zero. Efficiency calculations must define which energy input
and output are being compared.

Force varies with recruitment, activation timing, muscle length and loading
conditions. A **motor unit** consists of a motor neuron and the muscle fibres
it innervates. Recruiting more units can increase whole-muscle force without
changing the amplitude of each axon's action potentials. Smooth and cardiac
muscle share actin–myosin interactions but differ in organisation and control.
Smooth muscle is not simply skeletal muscle without visible stripes; its
calcium regulation and activation patterns differ.

## Nervous systems are diverse

Cnidarian nerve nets, ganglia and longitudinal nerve cords in many invertebrates,
and vertebrate central/peripheral systems illustrate different organisations.
Cephalisation concentrates sensory and integrating structures near a leading
end in many bilaterally organised animals. These arrangements reflect body
plans and behaviour, rather than a single scale of intelligence.

Sensory systems detect mechanical, chemical, light and other changes through
specialised receptor processes. A receptor converts a stimulus into a cellular
signal; subsequent neural pathways carry and interpret information. Adaptation
of a sensory response to a continuing stimulus differs from evolutionary
adaptation. Biological clocks add an internal timing component: daily rhythms
can persist under constant conditions while environmental cues entrain their
phase. State whether “adaptation” refers to receptor response, an individual's
adjustment or a heritable population feature.

## Hormones work through responsive target cells

An **endocrine hormone** enters internal transport fluid and can reach distant
cells. Only cells with suitable receptors and downstream machinery respond
in the relevant way. Peptide hormones often signal through surface receptors;
many steroid hormones act through intracellular receptors. The eventual
response can involve enzyme activity, transport, gene expression or several
of these together. “Hormones are always slow” is an unreliable rule: some
effects appear rapidly, while others require longer changes in cellular state.

The response depends on secretion, transport, breakdown, receptor abundance
and interactions with other signals. A high measured hormone concentration
does not guarantee a large effect at every target. Neuroendocrine cells
connect neural input to hormone release. Negative feedback can occur at
several levels of a regulatory axis, allowing the state of a target process
to influence upstream secretion. The reading on
[hormone action](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/37-2-how-hormones-work)
expands this distinction between signal and response.

## Reproduction integrates timing, resources and feedback

Reproduction includes gamete production, fertilisation, development and the
allocation of parental resources. Species vary in internal/external fertilisation,
sex organisation, reproductive cycles and parental investment. A mammalian
endocrine example provides a concrete feedback model without representing
all animals.

Hypothalamic GnRH stimulates pituitary release of gonadotropins, including
LH and FSH. These act on gonadal cells involved in steroid production and
gametogenesis. Gonadal signals feed back on hypothalamic/pituitary activity.
The sign and timing of feedback can change: sustained high oestrogen under
appropriate conditions can contribute to positive feedback leading to an LH
surge and ovulation. It would be incorrect to describe the entire reproductive
cycle as one unchanging negative-feedback loop. In male mammals, gonadal
and other signals also provide feedback governing endocrine activity and
sperm production. Consult the supporting account of
[hormonal reproductive control](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/43-4-hormonal-control-of-human-reproduction).

Energy availability, environmental timing and stress can influence reproduction.
These links explain why studying reproductive organs alone is insufficient.
The circulation carries signals, tissues need fuel, and neural pathways
provide information about surroundings. In a seasonal breeder, a prediction
about reproductive timing should therefore consider environmental cues and
physiological state rather than one hormone measurement alone.

## Bring the animal half together

Use a terrestrial animal escaping a threat as a final integration case. Trace
sensory detection, neural signalling, motor-unit recruitment, ATP use, oxygen
transport, heat production and water costs. Then ask which processes can
change immediately and which require sustained adjustment. For histology,
use described muscle and neural features as pre-lab practice; actual tissue
recognition must use the established slide collection. Your final explanation
should show coordinated mechanisms and their limits, not merely name systems.
Return to the [animal route](../index.qmd) for revision.
